[&_blockquote_p::after]:hidden","children":[["$","h3","h3-0",{"children":"Introduction"}],"\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":["Dr. Walter Anthony Rodney (1942–1980) was a pioneering Guyanese historian, political activist, and Pan-Africanist scholar whose intellectual and revolutionary work profoundly influenced the global Black Power movement, dependency theory, and post-colonial studies. Best known for his landmark book ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"How Europe Underdeveloped Africa"}],", Rodney bridged the gap between academic scholarship and grassroots political organizing. His life was defined by a commitment to the liberation of working-class and marginalized communities, particularly in the Caribbean and Africa. In his native Guyana, his efforts to unite the racially divided working class against the authoritarian regime of ",["$","$Lc","a-0",{"slug":"forbes-burnham","href":"/profiles/forbes-burnham","children":"Forbes Burnham"}]," made him a target of state surveillance, culminating in his tragic assassination in 1980 at the age of 38."]}],"\n",["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"Early Life and Academic Foundations in British Guiana"}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":["Born on March 23, 1942, in Georgetown, British Guiana, Walter Rodney grew up in a working-class household. His father, Edward Rodney, was a tailor, and his mother, Pauline Rodney, was a seamstress. His parents instilled in him a deep respect for education and social awareness. Edward Rodney was also an active supporter of the anti-colonial People's Progressive Party (PPP), led by ",["$","$Lc","a-0",{"slug":"cheddi-jagan","href":"/profiles/cheddi-jagan","children":"Cheddi Jagan"}],". Growing up in this highly politicized household, the young Walter was introduced early to the ideas of nationalist struggle and class consciousness, frequently accompanying his father to political meetings and distributions of party literature."]}],"\n","$Ld","\n","$Le","\n","$Lf","\n","$L10","\n","$L11","\n","$L12","\n","$L13","\n","$L14","\n","$L15","\n","$L16","\n","$L17","\n","$L18","\n","$L19","\n","$L1a","\n","$L1b","\n","$L1c","\n","$L1d","\n","$L1e","\n","$L1f","\n","$L20","\n","$L21"]}]]}],"$L22","$L23",false]}],"$L24"]}]
7:["$","script","script-0",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/2uyb8-0enc77-.js","async":true}]
8:["$","script","script-1",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/2z-jpqdx1wamk.js","async":true}]
9:["$","script","script-2",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/08pctmd9kh4qh.js","async":true}]
a:["$","$L25",null,{"children":["$","$26",null,{"name":"Next.MetadataOutlet","children":"$@27"}]}]
d:["$","p","p-2",{"children":"Rodney's intellectual brilliance became apparent early. He attended Queen's College, the premier secondary school for boys in Georgetown, where he excelled as an orator, debater, and student leader. His academic excellence earned him an open scholarship in 1960 to the University College of the West Indies (UCWI) in Mona, Jamaica. At UWI, Rodney studied history, graduating with First Class Honors in 1963. He was not only a brilliant student but also an active participant in campus politics, student government, and athletic activities."}]
e:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"London and the SOAS Years"}]
f:["$","p","p-3",{"children":["After graduating from UWI, Rodney traveled to the United Kingdom to pursue his doctorate in history at the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London. At SOAS, Rodney focused on African history, a field that was then dominated by Eurocentric perspectives. His dissertation, titled ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"A History of the Upper Guinea Coast 1545–1800"}],", was completed in 1966 when he was just 24 years old. Published by Oxford University Press in 1970, this study challenged standard colonial interpretations of the slave trade. Rodney argued that the transatlantic slave trade had a structurally devastating effect on African societies, disrupting local economies and social structures, while enriching European merchant capitalists. This research established Rodney as a formidable historian of Africa and set the stage for his subsequent work on dependency theory."]}]
10:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"The \"Groundings\" and the 1968 Rodney Riots in Jamaica"}]
11:["$","p","p-4",{"children":"In 1968, Rodney returned to Jamaica to take up a lectureship in African History at UWI Mona. Realizing that academic knowledge was often isolated from the public, Rodney sought to democratize history. He left the university campus to engage directly with the urban poor, Rastafarians, and unemployed youth in the slums of Kingston, such as Trench Town. In these informal meetings, which he termed \"groundings,\" Rodney shared lessons in African history, Black consciousness, and the realities of neocolonialism."}]
12:["$","p","p-5",{"children":["Rodney’s popularity among the marginalized masses alarmed the conservative Jamaican administration of Prime Minister Hugh Shearer. The government viewed his Marxist views and popularity among the Rastafari as a security threat. In October 1968, while Rodney was attending the Congress of Black Writers in Montreal, Canada, the Jamaican government declared him ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"persona non grata"}]," and banned him from re-entering the country."]}]
13:["$","p","p-6",{"children":["When news of Rodney's expulsion reached Kingston on October 16, 1968, UWI students organized a protest march to the Prime Minister's office. The demonstration quickly escalated as thousands of working-class citizens joined the students. The resulting civil unrest, known as the \"Rodney Riots,\" shut down parts of Kingston and resulted in property damage, clashes with police, and several deaths. Though the government suppressed the riots, the events marked a critical turning point in Jamaica's history, signaling the arrival of the Black Power movement in the Caribbean. The speeches and essays Rodney produced during this period were compiled into his influential book, ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Groundings with My Brothers"}]," (1969)."]}]
14:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"The black intellectual, the black academic must attach himself to the activity of the black masses. The black academic must be a spokesperson for the masses, translating their struggles and their aspirations into terms that are understood by those who hold power, but more importantly, he must return to the masses what they have given him.\""}],"\n"]}]
15:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"The Tanzanian Years and Ujamaa"}]
16:["$","p","p-7",{"children":"Following his exile from Jamaica, Rodney moved to Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, in 1969, where he joined the faculty of the University of Dar es Salaam. At the time, Tanzania was a hub of socialist and anti-imperialist thought, guided by President Julius Nyerere's policy of Ujamaa (African socialism). Dar es Salaam attracted liberation fighters, intellectuals, and activists from across the globe."}]
17:["$","p","p-8",{"children":["During his five years in Tanzania, Rodney participated in intense debates about African development. He sought to reconcile Marxism (scientific socialism) with Nyerere's traditional, communalist Ujamaa. In his essay ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Ujamaa and Scientific Socialism"}],", Rodney argued that Ujamaa could serve as a path to scientific socialism if it incorporated a class analysis of post-colonial society."]}]
18:["$","p","p-9",{"children":["It was during this productive period that Rodney wrote his masterwork, ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"How Europe Underdeveloped Africa"}]," (1972). In this book, Rodney argued that Africa’s modern challenges were not the result of internal failings, but rather the consequence of centuries of European exploitation. Using a historical materialist framework, he demonstrated how European powers extracted resources, labor, and capital from Africa to fuel their own industrial development, while systematically underdeveloping African institutions and economies."]}]
19:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"Return to Guyana and the Working People's Alliance (WPA)"}]
1a:["$","p","p-10",{"children":["In 1974, Rodney returned to Guyana, hoping to take up a position as Professor of History at the University of Guyana. However, the authoritarian government of ",["$","$Lc","a-0",{"slug":"forbes-burnham","href":"/profiles/forbes-burnham","children":"Forbes Burnham"}]," blocked his appointment. Undeterred, Rodney remained in Guyana and became a co-founder and leader of the Working People's Alliance (WPA), which formally transitioned into a political party in 1979."]}]
1b:["$","p","p-11",{"children":["The WPA, which included other radical figures like ",["$","$Lc","a-0",{"slug":"eusi-kwayana","href":"/profiles/eusi-kwayana","children":"Eusi Kwayana"}],", was a unique political force in Guyana because it sought to bridge the deep ethnic divide between the Afro-Guyanese and Indo-Guyanese working classes, which had been exploited by Burnham's PNC and ",["$","$Lc","a-1",{"slug":"cheddi-jagan","href":"/profiles/cheddi-jagan","children":"Cheddi Jagan"}],"'s PPP. Rodney’s message of cross-ethnic solidarity and democratic socialism posed a direct threat to Burnham's regime. Rodney traveled across the country, organizing rallies, teaching history, and mobilizing bauxite workers and sugar estate laborers."]}]
1c:["$","p","p-12",{"children":["Alongside other prominent figures like the poet ",["$","$Lc","a-0",{"slug":"martin-carter","href":"/profiles/martin-carter","children":"Martin Carter"}],", Rodney stood against the regime's repressive policies. As the WPA gained momentum, the Burnham government intensified its campaign of harassment against Rodney. He was arrested, put on trial on trumped-up arson charges, placed under constant surveillance, and subjected to physical threats. Despite the danger, Rodney refused to leave Guyana, declaring:"]}]
1d:["$","blockquote","blockquote-1",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"For the only people who can write the history of the working class are those who are prepared to take a stand in the struggle of the working class.\""}],"\n"]}]
1e:["$","h3","h3-6",{"children":"Assassination and Legacy"}]
1f:["$","p","p-13",{"children":"On the night of June 13, 1980, Walter Rodney was killed in Georgetown when a bomb exploded in a walkie-talkie he had been given by Gregory Smith, a sergeant in the Guyana Defence Force who was acting as a government agent. Rodney was 38 years old."}]
20:["$","p","p-14",{"children":"The Burnham administration claimed that Rodney had died when a bomb he was carrying to attack a prison exploded accidentally. However, his family, the WPA, and international observers maintained that it was a state-sponsored assassination. For decades, Rodney's family fought for justice. In 2014, the Guyanese government established a Commission of Inquiry into his death. The Commission's report, released in 2016 and formally adopted by the Guyanese Parliament in 2021, concluded that Rodney's death was a conspiracy involving the Guyanese state and that Gregory Smith was a state agent acting on behalf of the Burnham administration."}]
21:["$","p","p-15",{"children":"Walter Rodney’s legacy remains a guiding light for activists, scholars, and Pan-Africanists worldwide. His work demonstrated that academic scholarship must be paired with political action. Today, the Walter Rodney Foundation, established by his family, continues to promote his ideas of social justice, education, and human liberation."}]
